subject: Financial Literacy
chapter: Saving Money — The Piggy Bank Habit
title: Karan's Piggy Bank Dream
hook: A little money saved each day becomes a big treasure! Watch Karan's dream come true.

characters.name: Karan
characters.role: a boy who saves coins to buy a bicycle

characters.name: Grandmother
characters.role: Karan's wise grandmother who teaches the power of saving

slides.title: Karan's Piggy Bank Dream
slides.storyContext: Karan learns how small savings grow into big dreams.

image.alt: Karan's Piggy Bank Dream — Saving Money — The Piggy Bank Habit

slides.title: The Dream Bicycle
slides.storyContext: Karan is 10 years old. He loves cycling but his bicycle is old and rusty. One day, he sees his neighbor riding a shiny new bicycle. His heart aches—he wants one too! But when he asks his parents, they say, 'A new bicycle costs ₹5,000. That's a lot of money!' Karan feels sad. Then his grandmother calls him over. 'Karan beta, do you really want that bicycle?' Karan nods. 'Then I will teach you a secret—the magic of saving money.' Karan is curious: How can he get ₹5,000?

image.alt: The Dream Bicycle — Saving Money — The Piggy Bank Habit

slides.title: What Does "Saving" Mean?
slides.storyContext: Grandmother gives Karan a piggy bank (a small clay pig with a slot). 'Every rupee you don't spend, put it here. You're saving!' Karan asks, 'But grandmother, what IS saving?'

points.text: Saving means spending LESS than you earn or receive, and keeping the leftover money.
Money you save grows over time and can buy bigger dreams later.
A piggy bank, a box, or a bank account is a safe place to keep saved money.

example.problem: Karan gets ₹100 pocket money each week. He spends ₹70 on snacks and fun. How much can he save?

slides.inSimpleWords: Saving means keeping money instead of spending it all—like a treasure chest that grows bigger each day.

image.alt: What Does "Saving" Mean? — Saving Money — The Piggy Bank Habit

slides.title: Why Save? The Power of Saving
slides.storyContext: Grandmother tells Karan four reasons why saving is powerful. 'Listen carefully,' she says, settling in her chair with a warm cup of chai.

points.label: Reason 1: Big Dreams
points.text: A bicycle costs ₹5,000. You can't buy it with ₹100. But if you save ₹100 each month for 50 months, you have ₹5,000!

points.label: Reason 2: Emergencies
points.text: If your school uniform rips or you fall sick and need medicine, saved money helps without asking your parents every time.

points.label: Reason 3: No Borrowing
points.text: If you save, you don't need to borrow money from others and pay it back with extra cost (interest).

points.label: Reason 4: Freedom & Pride
points.text: Money you save is YOURS. You earned it and kept it. That feels amazing!

slides.inSimpleWords: Saving helps you buy big dreams, handle surprises, stay out of debt, and feel proud of yourself.

image.alt: Why Save? The Power of Saving — Saving Money — The Piggy Bank Habit

slides.title: How Much Should You Save? The Saving Rule
slides.storyContext: Karan asks, 'Grandmother, should I save all my pocket money and spend nothing?' She laughs gently. 'No beta, balance is important. There's a simple rule.'

points.text: A good saving rule for kids is: Save at least 1/3 (one-third) of your pocket money.
Example: If you get ₹300 pocket money, save ₹100 and spend ₹200.
Some people save 1/2 (half) or even more if they have a big goal.
The key: Save something from every rupee you receive—make it a HABIT.

example.problem: Karan gets ₹300 pocket money weekly. If he saves 1/3, how much does he save each week?
example.solution: 1/3 of ₹300 = ₹100 saved per week. He spends ₹200.

slides.inSimpleWords: Save at least 1/3 of every rupee you get—make it a habit, not an accident.

image.alt: How Much Should You Save? The Saving Rule — Saving Money — The Piggy Bank Habit

slides.title: Small Savings Add Up—The Magic of Time
slides.storyContext: Karan saves ₹100 every week. After one week, he has ₹100. After two weeks, ₹200. But grandmother shows him something magical—a chart of how his savings grow!

points.text: In just under a year, saving ₹100 weekly gives you almost ₹5,000!
This is the magic: small regular savings + TIME = big money.

example.problem: Karan saves ₹50 every day. After 100 days, how much has he saved?

slides.inSimpleWords: Save a little bit every day or week, and time turns it into a big amount—like magic!

image.alt: Small Savings Add Up—The Magic of Time — Saving Money — The Piggy Bank Habit

slides.title: Where to Keep Your Savings?
slides.storyContext: Karan asks, 'Grandmother, is a piggy bank safe? What if someone steals it?' Grandmother nods wisely. 'Good question. There are three places.'

points.label: Option 1: Piggy Bank at Home
points.text: Safe from your own spending! You can see your money grow. Good for kids learning to save.

points.label: Option 2: A Locked Box
points.text: A metal box with a key, hidden safely, where only you (and maybe a parent) can open it.

points.label: Option 3: A Bank Account
points.text: A real bank (like ICICI, SBI, Punjab National Bank) keeps your money safe and gives you interest (extra money!) on your savings.

slides.inSimpleWords: Keep savings in a piggy bank, a locked box, or best of all, a bank account that earns extra money.

image.alt: Where to Keep Your Savings? — Saving Money — The Piggy Bank Habit

slides.title: Karan's Year of Saving (Full Example)
slides.storyContext: Karan saves ₹100 every week. After 52 weeks (one year), he counts his piggy bank with his grandmother. How much does he have?

example.problem: ₹100 × 52 weeks = ? (This is the amount saved in one year.)
example.solution: ₹100 × 52 = ₹5,200. Karan now has enough for the ₹5,000 bicycle PLUS ₹200 extra!

image.alt: Karan's Year of Saving (Full Example) — Saving Money — The Piggy Bank Habit

slides.title: Your Turn: Savings Plan
slides.storyContext: You want to save ₹2,000 for a new school bag and shoes. You get ₹200 pocket money every month. If you save 1/2 of it each month, how many months until you reach your goal?

example.problem: You get ₹200/month. Save 1/2 = ₹100/month. Goal: ₹2,000. Months needed: ₹2,000 ÷ ₹100 = ?
example.solution: 20 months (about 1.5 years). Every rupee saved gets you closer!

image.alt: Your Turn: Savings Plan — Saving Money — The Piggy Bank Habit

slides.title: What We Learned
slides.storyContext: One year later, Karan rides his shiny new bicycle. He's so proud! Let's recap the lesson.

points.text: Saving means spending less than you earn and keeping the extra money.
You save for big dreams, emergencies, to avoid debt, and to feel proud.
Save at least 1/3 of your pocket money—make it a regular habit.
Small savings + time = big money. A little bit every day or week becomes a fortune!
Keep savings safe: in a piggy bank, a locked box, or best of all, a bank account.

slides.inSimpleWords: Save money regularly from what you get, and your dreams will come true. Start today!

image.alt: What We Learned — Saving Money — The Piggy Bank Habit

subject: Mathematics
title: Amir and Meera's Monsoon Journey
hook: Two cousins set out on a rainy adventure across the Indian countryside — and numbers follow them everywhere.

characters.name: Amir
characters.role: curious older cousin from the city

characters.name: Meera
characters.role: village girl who loves patterns and numbers

slides.title: We the Travellers - I
slides.storyContext: Amir arrives at his village cousins' home for the monsoon holidays. Meera greets him at the gate with a puzzled expression: she's counting raindrops falling into buckets arranged in the courtyard.

slides.title: The Monsoon Arrives
slides.storyContext: Dadaji assigns Amir and Meera a task: travel to the market to buy provisions for the week and bring back the bill. He gives them instructions written on a palm leaf, and Meera notices numbers everywhere — the cost of rice, the number of villages they must pass, the time on the old temple clock.
slides.inSimpleWords: Every journey we take, numbers guide us — the distance, the time, the money we spend.

slides.title: Numbers in Our World
slides.storyContext: At the first stop, a farmer shows them his harvest: 2,456 kg of rice he collected this season. Meera writes it down: 2,456. Amir looks confused. 'Is that really how we write it?'

points.label: Indian Place Value System
points.text: We write numbers using the Hindi place-value system: ones (ek), tens (das), hundreds (sau), thousands (hazar), ten thousands (das hazar), lakhs (lakh = 100,000). In 2,456: 2 is in the thousands, 4 in hundreds, 5 in tens, 6 in ones.

example.problem: The farmer says he has 2,456 kg of rice. Write this in expanded form.

slides.inSimpleWords: Each digit in a number has a place — ones, tens, hundreds, thousands. The place tells us what value that digit really has.

image.alt: Numbers in Our World — We the Travellers - I

slides.title: Reading Numbers in Words
slides.storyContext: Meera teaches Amir how villagers speak numbers aloud. '2,456 is "Two thousand, four hundred fifty-six," but we say it differently in Hindi — 'do hazaar, char sau, pachpan'.'

points.label: Speaking Numbers
points.text: Write each group of digits (thousands, hundreds, tens, ones) in words. 5,307 is 'five thousand, three hundred seven.'

slides.inSimpleWords: To read a big number out loud, say each group (thousands, hundreds, then tens and ones) in order.

image.alt: Reading Numbers in Words — We the Travellers - I

slides.title: Comparing Numbers
slides.storyContext: Two vegetable sellers at the market boast about their sales. One sold 3,456 kg of tomatoes, the other sold 3,546 kg. 'Who sold more?' asks Meera. Amir looks at the first digits — both are 3. Then he checks the second digit: 4 vs. 5. '3,546 is bigger!'

points.label: Comparing Step-by-Step
points.text: Start from the leftmost digit (thousands). If they're the same, move right to hundreds. Keep going until you find different digits — the bigger digit means the bigger number.

example.solution: Both start with 6. Hundreds: both 2. Tens: 3 vs. 4. So 6,243 > 6,234.

slides.inSimpleWords: To compare numbers, line up digits by place. Compare the leftmost first, then move right until you find the difference.

slides.title: Ordering Numbers
slides.storyContext: Dadaji asks them to write the prices of five items in order from cheapest to most expensive: 1,250 rupees (almanac), 890 (oil lamp), 2,100 (lantern), 1,100 (rope), 950 (salt). Meera arranges them: 890, 950, 1,100, 1,250, 2,100.

points.label: Ascending and Descending Order
points.text: Ascending = smallest to largest. Descending = largest to smallest. Compare step-by-step using place values.

example.problem: Order these from smallest to largest: 3,456; 2,100; 3,465; 2,999.

slides.inSimpleWords: Sort numbers by comparing thousands first, then hundreds, tens, and ones.

slides.title: Rounding Numbers
slides.storyContext: At the market, Meera learns that traders often round prices. A vendor says: 'These mangoes cost 1,249 rupees — I'll say 1,250 for simplicity.' Amir asks, 'Why round up?'

points.label: Rounding Rules
points.text: To round to the nearest ten: look at the ones digit. If ≥ 5, round up. If < 5, round down. To round to the nearest hundred: look at the tens digit. Same rule applies.

example.problem: Round 1,249 to the nearest 10 and nearest 100.
example.solution: Nearest 10: ones digit is 9 (≥5), so round up to 1,250. Nearest 100: tens digit is 4 (<5), so round down to 1,200.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rounding makes numbers simpler. If the last digit is 5 or more, go up. Less than 5, stay down.

image.alt: Rounding Numbers — We the Travellers - I

slides.title: The Market Bill
slides.storyContext: Meera and Amir collect their purchases. The shopkeeper writes the bill: Rice 2,456 kg @ 45 rupees/kg, Dal 340 kg, Oil 125 litres, Salt 250 kg. They need to check the total.

example.problem: The shopkeeper's bill shows: Rice (2 items): 1,200 + 856 rupees; Dal: 680 rupees; Oil: 450 rupees; Salt: 125 rupees. What is the total? Also express 1,200 + 856 in expanded form.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use place value to add large numbers step by step — ones with ones, tens with tens, hundreds with hundreds.

image.alt: The Market Bill — We the Travellers - I

slides.title: Your Turn: The Harvest Count
slides.storyContext: Dadaji gives them a final challenge before they leave the market: Three farmers compare harvests. Farmer A grew 5,234 kg of wheat. Farmer B grew 5,243 kg. Farmer C grew 4,999 kg. Meera writes them down and Amir orders them. Can you?

example.problem: Order these harvests from largest to smallest: 5,234; 5,243; 4,999. Also, round 5,243 to the nearest 100.
example.solution: Largest to smallest: 5,243 → 5,234 → 4,999. Rounding 5,243 to nearest 100: tens digit is 4 (<5), so round down to 5,200.

slides.inSimpleWords: Compare by looking at the leftmost different digits. When rounding, check the digit to the right of the place you're rounding to.

image.alt: Your Turn: The Harvest Count — We the Travellers - I

slides.title: What We Learned
slides.storyContext: Back home, Dadaji listens as Amir and Meera recount their journey. Meera says: 'Numbers were with us every step — in prices, distances, harvests.'

points.text: Numbers have place values: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, lakhs.
We can read numbers in words by saying each group aloud.
To compare numbers, look at the leftmost digit first. If equal, move to the next place value.
Ordering means arranging numbers from smallest to largest (or vice versa).
Rounding simplifies numbers: 5 or more rounds up, less than 5 rounds down.

slides.inSimpleWords: Place value is the foundation of reading, comparing, and using numbers in daily life.

image.alt: What We Learned — We the Travellers - I

subject: Mathematics
title: Amir and Meera's Return: Addition and Subtraction on the Road
hook: On the way back, Meera and Amir encounter problems that only addition and subtraction can solve.

characters.name: Amir
characters.role: curious older cousin from the city

characters.name: Meera
characters.role: village girl who loves patterns and numbers

slides.title: We the Travellers - II
slides.storyContext: Amir and Meera leave the market with heavy bags of provisions. On the way back, they face challenges: the bridge ahead is damaged, and they must travel through side villages instead. They need to calculate distances, add supplies, and subtract expenses.

image.alt: We the Travellers - II — We the Travellers - II

slides.title: The Detour
slides.storyContext: The main road is blocked. Meera pulls out Dadaji's old map showing three alternative routes: through the mango orchards (4 km), past the rice paddies (5 km), or along the river (6 km). To reach home, they must add and subtract distances.
slides.inSimpleWords: On their journey, Amir and Meera must solve real problems using addition and subtraction — just like we use math in daily life.

image.alt: The Detour — We the Travellers - II

slides.title: Addition with Large Numbers
slides.storyContext: Amir counts: 'From home to market, I walked 1,234 steps. Then from market to the vendor's stall, another 567 steps. How many total steps did I take to reach the vendors?' Meera sets up the addition on paper.

points.label: Column Addition (Place Value Method)
points.text: Write numbers one below the other, aligning by place value (ones below ones, tens below tens, etc.). Add each column from right to left. Carry the tens to the next column if a sum reaches 10 or more.

example.solution:
1234
+  567
------
  1801
Ones: 4+7=11 (write 1, carry 1). Tens: 3+6+1=10 (write 0, carry 1). Hundreds: 2+5+1=8. Thousands: 1. Answer: 1,801.

slides.inSimpleWords: To add large numbers, line them up by place value and add each column from right to left. If a column adds to 10 or more, carry the tens to the next column.

slides.title: Subtraction with Large Numbers
slides.storyContext: They started the journey with 5,000 rupees given by Dadaji. After buying provisions (cost: 3,311 rupees), Meera calculates: 'How much money is left?' Amir sets up the subtraction.

points.label: Column Subtraction (Borrowing)
points.text: Write the larger number on top, smaller below, aligned by place value. Subtract column by column from right to left. If the top digit is smaller than the bottom, borrow 10 from the next place and add it to the current digit.

example.solution:
5000
- 3311
------
  1689
Ones: 0 < 1, borrow from tens. Tens becomes 0-1=-1 (borrow again). Hundreds becomes 9 (after borrowing), 9-3=6. Tens: 9-1=8. Thousands: 4-3=1. Answer: 1,689 rupees left.

slides.inSimpleWords: When the top digit is smaller than the one below, borrow 10 from the next place to the left.

image.alt: Subtraction with Large Numbers — We the Travellers - II

slides.title: Adding Three or More Numbers
slides.storyContext: Along the detoured route, they pass three villages. Meera notes the prices of water pots at each: Village 1: 245 rupees, Village 2: 389 rupees, Village 3: 156 rupees. What's the total cost if they buy from all three?

points.label: Multi-Number Addition
points.text: Align all numbers by place value. Add column by column from right to left, carrying as needed. You can also add two at a time, then add the result to the next number.

example.solution:
245
  389
+ 156
------
  790
Ones: 5+9+6=20 (write 0, carry 2). Tens: 4+8+5+2=19 (write 9, carry 1). Hundreds: 2+3+1+1=7. Answer: 790 rupees.

slides.inSimpleWords: Adding multiple numbers is like adding two at a time — just keep carrying and adding each column.

slides.title: Checking Addition and Subtraction
slides.storyContext: Meera wants to check if her addition of 245 + 389 + 156 = 790 is correct. She uses the reverse: 790 - 245 - 389 should equal 156. Amir asks, 'How does that help?' 'If the answer is 156, I was right!'

points.label: Verification Methods
points.text: To check addition: use subtraction in reverse. Subtract one addend from the sum; if you get the other addend, you're correct. To check subtraction: add the result to the number you subtracted; you should get the original number.

example.solution:
1689
+ 3311
------
  5000
If the result is 5,000, the subtraction is correct. It is, so our answer was right!

slides.inSimpleWords: To check subtraction, add the answer back to the number you subtracted. You should get the original number.

image.alt: Checking Addition and Subtraction — We the Travellers - II

slides.title: Real-World Problem Solving
slides.storyContext: Dadaji sends word: 'A monsoon flood damaged 2,345 bales of hay from the northern field. The southern field has 4,789 bales. How many bales can still be used?' Meera sets up: 4,789 - 2,345.

points.label: Reading Word Problems
points.text: Identify what you know (the numbers) and what you're asked to find. Decide: is it addition or subtraction? 'How many more' or 'How many left' hints at subtraction. 'How many altogether' hints at addition.

example.problem: The northern field had 2,345 damaged bales. The southern field has 4,789 bales. How many bales can still be used from both fields?
example.solution: Damaged: 2,345. Usable from north: need this info (not given). Usable from south: 4,789. If the question is just about the south, answer is 4,789. If both, we need the northern total before damage.

slides.inSimpleWords: In word problems, find the numbers and decide: Do I add everything together, or subtract what's gone or used?

slides.title: The Journey Totals
slides.storyContext: By evening, Amir tallies the day: They walked 4 km through orchards, 5 km past rice paddies, and 3 km along the river (total distance). They spent 245 rupees on water, 156 on food, and 89 on rope. Meera adds up the distances, then subtracts the expenses from their remaining money.

example.problem: Distance: 4 + 5 + 3 = ? km. Expenses: 245 + 156 + 89 = ? rupees. If they had 1,689 rupees left, how much remains after these expenses?
example.solution: Distance: 4 + 5 + 3 = 12 km. Expenses: 245 + 156 + 89 = 490 rupees. Remaining: 1,689 - 490 = 1,199 rupees.

slides.inSimpleWords: Break multi-step problems into pieces: add the distances, add the expenses, then subtract.

slides.title: Your Turn: The Final Stretch
slides.storyContext: Dadaji asks one last puzzle before they rest: 'The journey from market to home is 12 km total. They've walked 4 km through orchards and 5 km past paddies. How many km remain? And if they spent 490 rupees already and have 1,199 rupees left, how much did Meera have to start this leg of the journey?'

example.problem: Distance walked: 4 + 5 = 9 km. Total distance: 12 km. Distance left: 12 - 9 = ? km. Money spent: 490. Money left: 1,199. Starting money for this leg: ?
example.solution: Distance left: 12 - 9 = 3 km. Starting money: 490 + 1,199 = 1,689 rupees.

slides.inSimpleWords: Two-step problems: solve one operation, then use that answer in the next.

slides.title: What We Learned
slides.storyContext: Amir and Meera finally reach home. Dadaji listens as they explain how addition and subtraction solved every problem on their journey.

points.text: Addition: Align by place value, add column by column from right to left, carry tens to the next place.
Subtraction: Align by place value, subtract column by column, borrow 10 from the next place if needed.
Check addition with subtraction in reverse; check subtraction by adding the answer back.
Multi-step problems: solve piece by piece, using one answer in the next step.
In real life, 'altogether' signals addition; 'left' or 'remaining' signals subtraction.

slides.inSimpleWords: Addition and subtraction are the tools we use to count what we have, what we spent, and what remains.
